reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The source set includes no survey-based adoption rate for defense. What the sources show instead is the institutional machinery through which AI enters U.S. defense programs. Per DIU, the Defense Innovation Unit describes itself as the Department's innovation pointman, with a mission to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power. Per Govini, its platform layer transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Per Janes, the firm applies advanced modeling and technology to connect millions of data points to uncover patterns, signals, and trajectories. The AI use cases visible in these sources are decision support, readiness forecasting, and intelligence analysis.

Vendor and money concentration runs through federal procurement records. Per SAM.gov, that system is the centralized source for finding and bidding on U.S. government contract opportunities, awards, and publishing subcontract reports. Per FPDS, the Federal Procurement Data System records DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level. Per USAspending, every federal award is downloadable and built on the FPDS feed. Per Govini, the platform tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy, publishing public scorecards on critical-technology spending. Per Silicon Valley Defense Group, the nonprofit monitors the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security, mapping the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space. DIU is the stated commercial on-ramp.

Government labs occupy a distinct position. Per The World of AI, the Government Labs section catalogues two individually verified organizations, Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China. State-funded government labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build and why. Both institutions can, in principle, command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. This matters for defense because sovereign budgets and compute are strategic inputs rather than commercial constraints.

The regulatory posture visible in the sources is a strict compliance environment around federal data. Per SAM.gov, the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information, and all individuals viewing, reproducing, or disposing of this information are required to protect it in accordance with 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2 CUI Policy. The system is subject to monitoring, and individuals found performing unauthorized activities are subject to disciplinary action including criminal prosecution. Per FPDS, the same GSA federal system is for official use only and subject to monitoring. The sources do not discuss AI-specific risk frameworks or ROI figures.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the takeaway is that the federal procurement record is the primary evidence base. SAM.gov carries solicitations, FPDS carries transaction-level contract actions, USAspending carries award data, and Govini builds decision science on that record. DIU is the stated gateway for commercial products. Janes offers validated intelligence for planning and forecasting. Because no adoption rate or ROI evidence appears in these sources, deployment decisions rest on procurement activity, vendor mapping, and intelligence tradecraft rather than measured survey statistics.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogs two government AI labs: Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China. According to the page, each classification is verified against a document the organization published about itself, with the source and date recorded, rather than assigned by keyword, model, or parent-company inheritance. The page notes the two labs represent different political economies: TII operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has released open models at the frontier of research, while Shanghai AI Laboratory is backed by national ministries and municipal government. Both institutions can, in principle, command infrastructure commitments such as compute and facilities that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
